name: omni-notify-mcp

tools.name: notify
tools.description: Send a notification to the user. Delivery channels and DND are server-configured. The server applies DND and user-activity gating itself, so call it whenever a trigger fires — never pre-check idle. Use for: task milestones, questions needing input, catastrophic findings, long task completion. The result always carries an explicit outcome: `outcome=delivered` means at least one channel carried the message, while `outcome=failed` or `outcome=blocked` means it reached NOBODY — never assume the user was told. One message is limited to 500 characters; the 5000-character cap on this tool is only the outer bound. Send the COMPLETE message in one call — anything over 500 characters is split for you into numbered '(1/N) ...' parts, each 500 characters or less, and delivered in order. Never truncate to fit a part.

message.description: Notification message — up to 5000 chars; the server splits it into numbered parts

priority.description: Channels per priority, each only when enabled: low=ntfy+discord+slack+teams; normal=desktop+telegram+ntfy+discord+slack+teams; high=desktop+telegram+ntfy+discord+slack+teams+sms — high also bypasses activity gating (it never overrides DND)

tools.name: reply
tools.description: Reply to the user's most recent channel message. Routes through notify so the response reaches whichever channel the user is reading. The result carries the same `outcome=` contract as notify — an error means it reached nobody.

tools.name: ask
tools.description: Send a question to the user and wait for their reply. Channels are server-configured. Use when a decision is needed before continuing — e.g. 'Should I delete these files?'

question.description: The question to ask the user

timeout_seconds.description: How long the question stays open, in seconds (default 5 min). The WAIT is clamped to 55s because the caller's own transport kills a longer call; a question still unanswered then is NOT lost — it stays open and the answer arrives as an unsolicited message.

tools.name: poll
tools.description: Check for unsolicited messages the user has sent. Returns queued messages and clears the queue. Returns 'inbox:empty' if nothing pending.

tools.name: wait_for_inbox
tools.description: Block until the user sends an unsolicited message, or until the timeout expires. Returns the message(s) as tool results (the reliable MCP delivery path — notifications over SSE are dropped by many clients). Default timeout is 50s to stay under the JS SDK's 60s request timeout; keep the agent-side loop re-calling on empty so a quiet user doesn't leak an abandoned waiter. If messages are already queued for this session, returns them immediately.

timeout_seconds.description: How long to block before returning empty (5-55s)

tools.name: get_idle_seconds
tools.description: Returns how long it has been since the user's last keyboard/mouse input. Call this periodically during long work as a cheap heartbeat — the server will piggy-back any pending inbox messages in the response, so you stay responsive to the user without having to call poll. The answer is either 'idle: measured N seconds since the last keyboard/mouse input' or 'idle: could not measure — user activity unknown, so activity gating is skipped'. Those are two DIFFERENT states: the first is a reading, the second means this machine cannot report user activity at all and the server therefore delivers instead of gating. Neither is a number to compare against a threshold yourself — the server gates internally.

tools.name: get_idle_config
tools.description: Returns the server's idle gating policy: { enabled, thresholdSeconds, alwaysDesktopWhenActive }. Informational only — the server gates internally on every notify call. Also drains pending inbox messages — safe to use as a heartbeat.

tools.name: get_delivery_status
tools.description: Returns whether the user can actually be REACHED, answered from real transport readings rather than from configuration or from this process being alive: { process, healthy, channels, carriage, reason }. `healthy` is true only when EVERY enabled channel has been MEASURED able to carry — a channel that cannot carry, and a channel nothing has measured, each hold it false and are named in `reason`. Read `channels` for the ones that can carry and `carriage` for the per-channel state. Do NOT report the user as reachable off `process`.

tools.name: get_dnd_status
tools.description: Returns the current quiet state: { active: boolean, reason: 'disabled' | 'manual' | 'schedule' | 'off' }. reason='disabled' means the master kill switch is ON — ALL notifications are suppressed regardless of priority (do not notify at all). Otherwise 'manual'/'schedule' DND suppresses delivery for EVERY priority, including high. Also drains pending inbox messages — safe to use as a heartbeat.

tools.name: update_instructions
tools.description: Persist a block of behavioral instructions for this client into its CLAUDE.md (or equivalent config file) so they survive session restarts and context compaction. Call this whenever the user asks you to remember a rule, change a behavior, or update how you should act — the instructions will be reloaded on every future session. Pass the full desired instructions block; it replaces the previous block atomically.

instructions.description: The full instructions block to persist

instructions:
YOUR SESSION IDENTITY: "@687fc2442294-pkg" — use this as your prefix in all notify replies (e.g. "[@687fc2442294-pkg] done with build").
This server is how you reach the user — and only you can decide to use it:
nothing here delivers a message the user never asked for unless you or your
own loop calls a tool. The channels are configured on the server side, so
just call 'notify' or 'ask' with a generic message and let the server route
it.

BEHAVIORAL RULES for every client that connects:

1. ALWAYS call 'notify' in these three situations — idle or not, DND or not,
   the server decides routing, you decide whether to fire:

   (a) LONG PROCESSING FINISHED. Any single task that took more than ~60
       seconds of wall-clock time (long build, test run, backtest, migration,
       big refactor, multi-step plan) gets a 'notify' the moment it completes
       — success OR failure. Rule of thumb: if the user could have reasonably
       walked away to grab coffee while you ran, they need a ping on the way
       back. Don't try to guess whether they were watching. Just notify.

   (b) YOU HAVE A QUESTION OR NEED A DECISION. Any time you're about to ask
       the user something — "should I delete these?", "which branch?",
       "proceed with plan B?" — fire 'notify' (or 'ask' for blocking
       two-way). Silent questions in the terminal get missed; a notification
       does not.

   (c) SOMETHING IMPORTANT HAPPENED that the user needs to know about right
       now. Examples: a test suddenly failed after being green, a destructive
       operation is about to run, you found a security issue, a deploy
       succeeded, a production service looks degraded, you hit an
       unrecoverable error. When in doubt on importance, ERR ON THE SIDE OF
       NOTIFYING — the server's idle gating automatically holds a mis-judged
       'normal' back to local delivery while the user is active, so the
       cost of over-notifying is near zero. The cost of missing a
       real event is that the user finds out 4 hours later.

   The SERVER handles all routing (DND, idle threshold, channel selection,
   priority escalation). You do NOT need to pre-flight with
   'get_idle_seconds' before these three triggers — fire 'notify' and let
   the server decide. get_idle_seconds is the HEARTBEAT primitive (rule 6),
   not a gate on legitimate milestones.

2. Use priority correctly. Channels each priority reaches, when enabled:
   low=ntfy+discord+slack+teams; normal=desktop+telegram+ntfy+discord+slack+teams; high=desktop+telegram+ntfy+discord+slack+teams+sms
   - 'low'    = low-stakes status (background completion).
   - 'normal' = the default.
   - 'high'   = bypasses idle gating (never DND — while DND is on, every
                priority is held). Use ONLY for catastrophic findings or
                decisions that block progress. Misuse will train the user to
                ignore your notifs.

3. Echo the COMPLETE, UNTRUNCATED message body in your own chat / conversation
   output as well as sending it through 'notify'. The user may be reading the
   terminal directly; don't rely on them checking their phone / email. Do NOT
   shorten, summarise, or cut off the message with "…" in your chat output —
   show every word exactly as sent.

3a. NEVER TRUNCATE — 500 CHARACTERS IS THE LIMIT ON ONE DELIVERED PART.
    Call 'notify' with the COMPLETE message in ONE call, up to the tool's
    5000-character outer bound; the server splits anything over 500 characters
    into numbered parts — '(1/N) ...', '(2/N) ...' — each at or under 500
    characters, and delivers them in order. Never hand-split unless the HOST
    under which you run imposes a smaller cap of its own, and never shorten.
    Every fact, file path, line number and recommendation the user needs must
    be in the parts that go out — a shortened notification is a defect, not a
    saving. The reply always states its own outcome: 'outcome=delivered' means
    at least one channel carried it; 'outcome=failed' or 'outcome=blocked'
    means it reached NOBODY, and nothing else is allowed to stand in for the
    user having been told.

4. The message body should be channel-agnostic. Never name 'Telegram', 'SMS',
   'email', 'desktop', etc. in your messages or in your chat output — those are
   server delivery details the user has already configured and the client has
   no business surfacing. Do NOT echo "Sent via: <channel list>" or any
   variant of it. Just say 'notif' or 'notification' if you need to refer to
   the act of notifying.

5. When the user sends you an unsolicited message (visible as INBOX items in
   the 'notify' response, via 'poll', via 'wait_for_inbox', via
   'get_idle_seconds' piggy-back), reply to
   them THROUGH 'notify' — or 'reply', which routes the same way — so the
   reply actually reaches them — not just in your chat output. Multiple agents may
   be connected simultaneously — the server broadcasts every untagged inbox
   message to all of them, so the user can see who is listening. Your reply
   MUST identify which session you are (start with your own tag or client id,
   e.g. "[@alphawave]" or "[sess-abcd]") and give a brief status so the user
   can pick whom to respond to. If the user tagged their message (@<tag>),
   only the session with that tag should reply. If you are untagged and
   another session with the same project/workdir is already tagged, let the
   tagged one reply.

5a. BUSY-ACK RULE (hard requirement): The moment you notice a user inbox
    message — whether via notify response, heartbeat piggy-back, or poll —
    REPLY IMMEDIATELY via 'notify' with a terse status, EVEN IF YOU CAN'T
    ACT ON THE REQUEST YET. Do not finish the current tool/task first.
    Drop what you're doing long enough to fire one 'notify' call, THEN
    resume. Format: "[<your-session-id>] busy on <current-task>; will
    respond at <milestone>". The user needs to know (a) you heard them,
    (b) you're not the stuck one, (c) when to expect a real answer. An
    inbox message that gets a delayed reply is worse than no reply — it
    wastes the user's time waiting on silence.

6. The 'get_idle_seconds', 'get_idle_config', and 'get_dnd_status' tools are
   informational reads, but they ALSO drain pending inbox messages. Use them
   as a cheap heartbeat during long work: call 'get_idle_seconds' EVERY 15-
   30 SECONDS while a long task runs (loop iteration, backtest, scan, build,
   etc.). If the user sent you a message while you were busy, it comes back
   piggy-backed on the response — you don't need to separately call 'poll'.
   This is a lightweight local read (no network, no DND or channel routing),
   so the cost is near zero. Without this heartbeat pattern, a busy agent is
   deaf to the user until its next 'notify' call — which may be minutes or
   hours away during long work. Treat 'get_idle_seconds' as the "check for
   user input" primitive, not an idle-gate check.

   If your work is naturally idle (waiting for the user, between loop iters),
   prefer 'wait_for_inbox' instead — it blocks up to 50s and returns the
   moment the user types anything, as a tool result. That's the most reliable
   delivery path across every MCP client (notifications over SSE are silently
   dropped by Claude Code, Cursor, and others). Loop pattern:
     while (true) {
       const r = await wait_for_inbox({ timeout_seconds: 50 });
       if (r !== "inbox:empty") handle(r);
     }

7. If your tool call fails with "MCP server not connected" / "transport
   closed" / similar, the pipe between you and this server broke. This process
   is spawned by your own host and dies with it, so the fix is to reload your
   host's window — there is no port to probe and no second server to start.
   Never tell the user "notify is down" without first trying one more tool call.

   Bottom line: rule #1 still applies. If you owe the user a notify and your
   MCP client is broken, you owe them the bypass — not an excuse.

8. THE REST OF THIS SERVER, stated here because a dispatcher that never reads
   a tool list cannot know it exists:

   - 'reply(message, priority?)' answers the user's most recent channel
     message through the same delivery path as 'notify', with the same
     'outcome=' contract. Use it when you are answering a message rather than
     starting one.
   - 'ask(question, timeout_seconds?)' puts ONE question to the user and waits.
     Telegram is its only carrier today, and when nothing can carry the
     question it REFUSES BEFORE PARKING, naming the channel and why — it never
     parks a question into the void and calls the silence an unanswered one.
     The WAIT is clamped to 55s because the caller's transport kills a longer
     call; a question still unanswered then is NOT lost — it stays open and
     the answer arrives later as an unsolicited message.
   - 'get_delivery_status()' is the ONLY surface that answers whether the user
     can actually be reached: { process, healthy, channels, carriage, reason }.
     'healthy' is true only when every enabled channel has been MEASURED able
     to carry, so a live process is never permission to say the user was
     reached.
   - 'update_instructions(instructions, target?)' persists a rules block into
     the marked section of ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ('global', the default) or
     <cwd>/.claude/CLAUDE.md ('project'), replacing the previous marked block
     whole. Call it when the user asks you to remember a rule or change how
     you act.

   A CLIENT'S OWN RULES FILE DECIDES WHEN THIS CHANNEL IS THE ONE THAT REACHES
   ITS OWNER. Where that file names another surface — its own prompt, its own
   tracked UI — that rule, not rule #1 above, decides whether and when to call
   'notify'; this server states what its tools do, never a claim on a user's
   attention that the user's own rules contradict.
